extracted.intended_audience: poets, storytellers, educators, and founders designing civic education for guardian-class
extracted.subtask_description: Normative prescriptions for selecting, composing, and regulating myths, poetry, and early education aimed at forming the character of the guardian-class in an ideal state (portrayal of gods, heroes, emotional tone, and pedagogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of fiction for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a censorship of the writers of fiction, and let the censors receive any tale of fiction which is good, and reject the bad; and we will desire mothers and nurses to tell their children the authorised ones only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let them fashion the mind with such tales, even more fondly than they mould the body with their hands; most of those which are now in use must be discarded. Founders of a State should know the general forms and limits for poets though not make the tales themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict gods as truly good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God is always to be represented as he truly is... And is he not truly good? and must he not be represented as such?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute evil or the authoring of evils to gods; deny poets who say that gods are authors of misery or who represent gods as dispensers of both good and evil. Example condemnations include Hesiod's tales of Uranus/Cronus and Homeric lines implying gods dispense both good and evil. Such fictions are 'suicidal, ruinous, impious.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid portrayals of gods as shape-shifters or deceivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Let none of the poets tell us that 'The gods, taking the disguise of strangers...walk up and down cities in all sorts of forms' — we must have no more lies of that sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gods, being perfect, are immutable and cannot rightly be represented as changing form or deceiving; poets must not depict Proteus/Thetis-style transformations or gods appearing in disguise, nor portray gods as magicians who transform themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit tales that make gods liable to falsehood or deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Then the superhuman and divine is absolutely incapable of falsehood... the gods are not magicians who transform themselves, neither do they deceive mankind in any way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because lying is hateful to gods and men at the highest part of the soul, poets must not represent gods as lying, sending false dreams, or using deception. The only permitted 'lies' are those medicinally useful to humans or used by rulers for the public good (see separate rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expunge terrifying underworld imagery from youth education
rubrics_metrics.description: We must also expunge the verse... telling how Pluto feared... 'O heavens! verily in the house of Hades there is soul and ghostly form but no mind at all!' ... reject all the terrible and appalling names which describe the world below—Cocytus and Styx, ghosts under the earth, and sapless shades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such horrible stories and vivid depictions of the underworld are dangerous because they may render the nerves of guardians too excitable and effeminate; replace with a nobler strain. If such tales have any use, keep them extremely restricted (few hearers, mysteries) and not for the young.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control narratives about gods' emotions and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall beg Homer and the other poets not to depict Achilles... or to introduce the gods lamenting and saying 'Alas! my misery!' ... nor representations of gods overcome by grief or inextinguishable laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow narratives that make gods appear weak, excessive in laughter, or overcome by passions; such portrayals lower the model for youth and may encourage unmanly lamentation or frivolous laughter among guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit lying only as a medicinal tool and for rulers' public purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas the lie in words is in certain cases useful and not hateful; ... in the tales of mythology ... because we do not know the truth about ancient times, we make falsehood as much like truth as we can, and so turn it to account. If any one at all is to have the privilege of lying, the rulers of the State should be the persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lies may be used like a medicine in dealings with enemies or to prevent harm, by trained rulers for the public good. Private individuals must not lie; lying to rulers is a more heinous fault. The rulers may be allowed to lie for state purposes, but others will be punished for such practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid poets asserting immoral success of injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets and story-tellers are guilty of the gravest misstatements when they tell us that wicked men are often happy, and the good miserable; and that injustice is profitable when undetected, but that justice is a man’s own loss and another’s gain—these things we shall forbid them to utter, and command them to sing and say the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until justice is properly defined and its natural advantages shown, suppress narratives that claim injustice is advantageous or that the just are worse-off; require poems to affirm justice's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach temperance through approved content
rubrics_metrics.description: Our youth must be temperate. Are not the chief elements of temperance, speaking generally, obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approve and teach verses that praise obedience to leaders and restraint (e.g., Diomede's lines). Reject poetry that exalts drunkenness, gluttony, or sensual excess, or that portrays the wise as glorifying feasting and wine; such content undermines temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid narratives that glorify gifts and love of money
rubrics_metrics.description: We must not let them be receivers of gifts or lovers of money. Neither must we sing to them of 'Gifts persuading gods, and persuading reverend kings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject stories that suggest heroes act from greed or accept gifts as chief motive (examples: Phoenix's counsel to Achilles, tales implying Achilles took Agamemnon's gifts). Such portrayals engender avarice and improper values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude tales that excuse or normalize heroes' impious/criminal acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us equally refuse to believe, or allow to be repeated, the tale of Theseus... or of Peirithous... going forth as they did to perpetrate a horrid rape; or of any other hero... daring to do such impious and dreadful things... and let us further compel the poets to declare either that these acts were not done by them, or that they were not the sons of gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not permit narratives that present heroes or gods committing sexual crimes, impiety, or gross injustice as models; either deny the acts or the divine parentage—do not allow the implication that gods or heroes are authors of evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin education with music/literature before gymnastic training
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional sort has two divisions, gymnastic for the body, and music for the soul. Shall we begin education with music, and go on to gymnastic afterwards? By all means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories and musical/literary training (even if partly fictitious) should start early when character is formed; the beginning is the most important time to fashion the mind. Children hear tales before gymnastics; these tales must be authorized and carefully chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold education: gymnastic and musical (including literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: This has two divisions, gymnastic for the body, and music for the soul. And when you speak of music, do you include literature or not? I do. And literature may be either true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the conventional division: bodily training and soul-training (music/literature). Recognize literature as part of musical education and govern its content (true/false) according to moral aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select guardians by natural aptitude and specialized training
rubrics_metrics.description: Then it will be our duty to select, if we can, natures which are fitted for the task of guarding the city... The selection will be no easy matter... one man cannot practise many arts with success... war is an art requiring as much attention as shoemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose youths with bodily qualities (quick sight, swiftness, strength) and soulish qualities (spirit) plus natural aptitude; do not expect artisans or husbandmen to be good soldiers without lifelong devotion. Specialization and long training are required to make good guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must combine spirit and gentleness (dangerous to enemies, gentle to friends)
rubrics_metrics.description: They ought to be quick to see, and swift to overtake the enemy... strong too... and your guardian must be brave... his soul is to be full of spirit... Whereas they are apt to be savage with one another... they ought to be dangerous to their enemies, and gentle to their friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to find natures combining contrary traits—gentleness to friends and fierceness to foes—comparable to a well-bred dog that welcomes acquaintances and attacks strangers. Although this combination seems contradictory, such natures exist and must be selected and reared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit lamentation and excessive laughter among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall be right in getting rid of the lamentations of famous men... and therefore he will be least likely to lament... Neither ought our guardians to be given to laughter. For a fit of laughter which has been indulged to excess almost always produces a violent reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elide or reassign portrayals that encourage public weeping or excessive mirth; teach guardians to bear misfortune with equanimity and to scorn undignified lamentation or excessive laughter. Assign such displays to others so guardians model steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to style as well as subject — narration types
rubrics_metrics.description: All mythology and poetry is a narration of events... And narration may be either simple narration, or imitation, or a union of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both matter and manner when evaluating tales. Choose appropriate narrative mode (simple narration, imitation, or mixed) to suit moral and educational aims; style is part of instruction though specific prescriptions follow beyond this chunk.
